abertura-1.text: PART I
abertura-1.subtitle:
WHEN THE WORLD BEGINS FROM WITHIN
Experience Before Action

abertura-1.text: There are things that do not appear immediately. They do not announce themselves, do not ask permission, and do not explain themselves. And yet they hold everything that comes after.

Before any attempt to help, before any well-placed word, before even knowing what to do, there is a silent territory. A place where the child’s experience begins to take shape. An inside that is rarely seen — but that never stops working.

For many children, the world does not arrive as a ready-made idea. It arrives as pure sensation. Light, sound, touch, temperature, movement — all approaching at once, in layers that overlap without warning.
The day does not present itself organized; it simply happens. And as it happens, something inside the child must receive, sustain, and order that flow in order to keep being there.
This work is invisible. It happens before intention. Before language. Before any response that can be recognized from outside.

The body feels. The system tries to follow. Sometimes it manages. Sometimes it reaches its limit. When that limit is reached, something overflows: a sudden cry, a withdrawal, a repeated gesture, a body trying to contain the sound, the light, the excess.
What is seen from outside is usually called behavior. What is not seen is the immense effort to maintain some continuity from within.

This first part of the book is an invitation to slow the gaze. Not to analyze or correct — but to recognize. To draw close to what has always been happening beneath what breaks through to the surface.
Here, the starting point is not what needs to change in the child — but what needs to be held by the adult.

The invitation is to understand that intensity can be a request for regulation. That withdrawal can be an intelligent form of protection. That repetition can be a legitimate attempt to maintain structure when the surroundings shift.
None of this is empty. Everything responds to an inner logic — even if silent.
In accepting to enter that territory, something also changes in whoever cares. The urgency diminishes. The curiosity grows.

The question stops being “how do I make this stop?” and begins to transform into “what is this telling?” The relationship starts to organize itself more through presence than through the attempt at control.

This part of the book moves through those initial layers: the impact of the news, the feeling of the skin, the body searching for ground, the direction lost in the crisis, the effort to make sense in the chaos.
These are not only concepts. They are lived experiences — the ones that shape the child’s mood, availability, and the brightness in their gaze across the day.
Nothing here asks for hurry. Nothing resolves all at once. This is only the beginning of the crossing.
The ground begins to be built from within — in the way the adult observes, responds, and remains.
From here on, every page is permission to recognize what the child has always been communicating — even when there were still no words for it.
Here, the world begins from within.

cap-1.text: There are mornings that open slowly, like so many others that came before, with no sign that the familiar pulse is about to shift. The house follows its own rhythm. The gestures happen within what is expected.

For a brief moment, everything remains the same. Until a candid conversation — or the attentive presence of someone who observes — brings the understanding that life does not come undone. It only finds another form.
An almost invisible movement that asks of whoever cares, a new internal place to exist.
The news that arrives carries force and silence. There is an adjustment from within, like an unexpected clarity crossing a crack you did not know existed.
Sometimes that light is soft; at other times, too intense. But it always reveals more than it hides.

It is common that, in that moment, the heart tries to give shape to what it cannot yet reach. A delicate feeling arises, difficult to name, that asks for care and time. A new territory, where the hands still search for where to land.

Every beginning carries its own jolt. With it come silent questions about the path that opens. There is, for a brief moment, an intimate farewell — not of the real child, but of the image that walked beside you until there.

That small grief does not linger. It lasts the time needed for the gaze to find another resting point: when it stops searching for the imagined child and begins to recognize the child who exists, whole and present.
It is at that point that the diagnosis finds its place. It does not arrive to close questions — but to offer direction.
It gives a name to a truth that was already there, still without words. The reactions, the distances, and the intensities are now read as singular forms of receiving the world.
From that new gaze, what once seemed like a sentence transforms into a reading key. The path does not become shorter — but becomes possible to travel with more safety.

Acceptance begins to settle when something organizes from within. When you recognize that you can breathe in the middle of the path, that you do not need to hide what you feel, that you can remain. That you can be safe harbor.
In that movement, the internal narrative changes. The chapter of silent grief gives way to a gesture of approach — not the one that observes from a distance, but the one that offers itself entirely.
It is when the gaze finds the real child and, even without words, something communicates with clarity: I see you; I am here; we go on together.
Understanding this is perceiving that the path has widened. Having a path — even with curves and pauses — is different from being lost. The path holds, gives breath, and brings closer.
Nothing closes here. This is only the first gesture of a deeper encounter.

From here, that gaze needs to take form in daily life. Not through great movements, but through minimal, nearly invisible gestures that attune the relationship and offer the child an internal space where she can land.
It is those silent details that hold what understanding inaugurates.
When the gaze finds a wider place to rest, the relationship breathes. And in that breath, a readiness is born that holds — the first gesture of shared presence.

cap-1.title: SMALL PRACTICES
cap-1.subtitle: Beginning of the gaze and presence

items.title: Stopping to see
items.text: Once a day, pause for a minute. Look at your child without saying anything, without correcting, without anticipating. Just see.

items.title: Being before doing
items.text: When you feel the urge to guide, explain, or lead, wait a few seconds and ask inwardly: what is happening right now?

items.title: Naming the moment
items.text: At some point in the day, say just to yourself: we are here. Do not explain. Do not complete.

items.title: Closing with presence
items.text: At the end of the day, remember a moment when you were present, even if briefly. Do not evaluate. Do not judge. Recognize.

cap-1.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-1.subtitle: The window of the new gaze
body: This exercise places side by side two times: what was imagined and what now reveals itself.
Separate two sheets of paper. On the first, write a letter to the expectation that accompanied you. Thank its presence and allow it to withdraw.
On the second, write to the real child, with the truth that her gestures reveal today, without hurry.
When you finish, ask softly — or just inwardly: what are my eyes learning to see now?

cap-1.text: Keep the two sheets together. With time, you will notice that the world did not shrink; it only gained depth.
When that first internal shift rests, and the imagined image gives way to the real child, a ground is born where feeling begins to reveal itself. That is where we follow.

cap-2.text: The body is the territory where everything begins before gaining a name.
Long before the word exists, experience already pulses there — as a sensitive field where lights, sounds, textures, and movements present themselves at the same time, with their own force.
It is in that intimate space that the world first reveals itself to the child. For her, the body is not only the house she inhabits; it is the portal through which everything enters.
And what enters arrives whole. Without pause, without filter, without immediate translation.

The light that for an adult is simply brightness can become too intense. Background noise changes in size and occupies more space. The texture of clothing demands constant attention, and touch arrives as presence — not as detail.
Every stimulus finds the body in a state of openness — and there begins a silent work of translation.

When the world arrives this way, each step that follows is born from that first sensory contact. Movement, the search for support, the need for rhythm emerge as attempts by the body to organize itself, find axis, and create contour.
The child responds as she can: with movement, with silence, with withdrawal, or with intensity.

Sometimes she runs, spins, or rocks herself to find again an axis that the environment displaced. At other times she needs to retreat and curl inward to recompose internally. That constant adjustment demands continuous effort and consumes an energy that is rarely visible from outside.
With time, the attentive gaze begins to perceive function where before it saw strangeness.

The rocking of the trunk helps to find stability again. Covering the ears protects against sounds that arrive without contour. Repeating movements offers predictability when the world varies too quickly.
When that gaze softens and accompanies the cadence of the body, something reorganizes in the relationship. The gesture stops being read as excess and begins to be recognized as language.

The child does not perceive the environment in a neutral way; she perceives it with her own intensity. In recognizing this, the manner of approaching changes. Whoever cares stops trying to correct and begins to learn to observe.
Listening, here, is not technique. It is presence. It is observing without hurry, accompanying the child’s time, breathing together, and noticing signals that went unperceived before.
In perceiving the effort she makes to adjust to what arrives, small gestures around her begin to transform the experience.
A softer light calms. A firm touch orients. A deep embrace organizes.
Sometimes, just the gaze — a silent invitation that communicates availability.
When that gaze meets hers, something reveals itself in small adjustments: here it tightens, here it weighs, here it is necessary to stop, here it is possible to find oneself again.
From that approach, the adult stops being only the one who welcomes and becomes the place where the child finds stability. A safe space where the body can, gradually, loosen its internal defenses.
When that rest arrives, everything internally breathes a little better.
That is why, before names and long before words, there exists something more essential: shared presence.
Something begins to communicate in that encounter — in the silence that gives space, in the movements that seek balance, in the breath that attunes to the one alongside.
The child has always conversed in that idiom. A silent idiom, prior to explanation, that the body finds before even understanding what it feels.
When the adult draws close to what she feels, the world decelerates. In that brief interval, an understanding is born that needs no voice — only a presence that holds.

items.title: The gentle scanner
items.text: When entering a space, allow the gaze to move through the environment slowly. Observe lights, sounds, and textures that may speak loudly to the child’s body. Sometimes adjusting a single detail already restores comfort.

items.title: Less input, more peace
items.text: When agitation appears, try removing a stimulus before adding words. A softened light or a turned-off device can restore calm in a few moments.

items.title: The anchor word
items.text: Choose together a light word — a silent door. When something tightens, that word can be said or shown. It signals the need for pause, without explanations. With time, the child recognizes that she can step away safely.

items.title: The pause at the door
items.text: Before entering a new environment, pause for a few seconds. That simple gesture gives the body time to prepare.

cap-2.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-2.subtitle: The map of layers
body: This exercise invites you to feel, for a moment, what happens when different stimuli arrive together.
Sit in a quiet place. Breathe until you find a comfortable rhythm. Choose three simple stimuli: a soft sound, a discreet touch, a small variation of light.
Allow them to happen almost simultaneously. Do not intensify anything. Only observe how each stimulus tries to draw attention and how the body seeks to follow them.
Then pause. Breathe deeply. Let everything settle.

Notice the difference between the moment when everything was arriving together and the moment when each stimulus finds its place. That transition — from accumulation to contour — is a portrait of the inner path the child travels every day.

cap-2.text: For some children, the world does not arrive by excess. It arrives by simultaneity. Recognizing this is the first gesture of care.
When feeling finds rest, a new space opens. It is in that interval that movements begin to find voice — small gestures that tell what does not yet fit in words. That is where we follow.

cap-3.text: There is a moment when experience stops being only impact and begins to gain form. Not because the world has changed — but because something in the child begins to organize itself as reference.

An inner point that says, without words: I am here. Before any recognizable emotion, before any intentional action, there exists that silent knowing. A knowing that does not pass through idea, nor through language, nor through explanation. It is born from the sensation of weight, of force, of resistance, of contact.

It is in that encounter that presence begins to be built. When that reference is not yet firm, everything arrives loose. The child feels, but does not locate herself. She moves, but does not lean. The space seems too wide, and the experience itself difficult to inhabit. Something is missing that indicates where she begins, where she ends, where she can land.
In those moments, the search is not for stimulus. It is for limit.

That silent request appears in the world as a search for contour: the desire to lean against something, to press, to find something that resists. In autistic functioning, that movement does not arise as excess — but as an attempt at bodily organization, a way to gather what does not yet hold itself together.

The child approaches what offers resistance — the wall that does not yield, the cushions that squeeze, the embrace that holds. She leans, pushes, sustains. Not to agitate herself — but to find herself. It is a legitimate effort to integrate parts that do not yet recognize themselves as a whole.
When she finds pressure, something gains contour. When she finds resistance, something is delimited.

This process is precise. Little by little, the capacity to recognize herself internally emerges. To feel where she is without having to look. To hold a position without getting lost. To exist as a continuous unit, even when the environment varies.

That learning happens in fine layers, repeated throughout the day. Each experience of support leaves an inner trace. Each predictable contact builds a margin. Each sustained gesture offers a little more clarity.
With time, it becomes unnecessary to gather everything all the time. A more stable base begins to form, allowing the world to approach without crossing too deeply.
In some moments, that search for contour finds its answer in the encounter with another.

A firm embrace, announced and respected — when welcome — does not arise as a generic affective gesture, but as bodily reference. The shared weight helps to draw limits, organizes the inner sensation, and allows the child to feel: here I am.
To hold is not to contain. It is to offer conditions for the experience to find form.
When the limit comes from outside with care, something organizes internally. Presence gains consistency. Movements become more economical. Energy finds direction. The inner space stops leaking.
The contour that forms is alive. It adjusts as the child grows, as the environment changes, as new experiences accumulate. It is a limit that holds.

In some moments, movement helps to confirm that presence. Small displacements, changes of position, gentle rocking. Not to lose reference — but to reaffirm it. Movement, here, says: I continue here, even in transition.

When that base begins to firm up, something essential happens. The child begins to be present before needing to react. The world can arrive without crossing completely. Sensation finds margin. Impact finds support.

Some self-regulatory behaviors — like seeking pressure, rhythm, or firm contact — are often read as unnecessary agitation. When the gaze aligns with the inner need, the meaning reveals itself: it is a request for ground. Limits are sought so that it becomes possible to feel — and then to calm.
The adult’s role in that process is to offer conditions for that organization to happen. A stable environment. Firm support. A predictable presence that neither invades nor abandons.
When that kind of holding is available, something settles deeply. The child no longer needs to defend herself from the world all the time. She can, finally, be.
Before understanding what she feels, before organizing emotions or actions, it is necessary to know where one is.
That knowing is not born from explanation. It is born from contour.
When that localization is established, the world stops crossing without warning. The child can then inhabit her own body — and it is from that inner place that everything else becomes possible.

items.title: Offering support that resists
items.text: When the environment seems unstable, seeking something that does not yield can help. Pushing against a wall, resting weight on an adult, or holding a firm position favors bodily organization.

items.title: Firm and predictable contact
items.text: Deep, clear, and respectful touches — always announced — help when everything seems loose. A tight embrace, when well received, can restore contour and calm at the same time.

items.title: An environment that holds
items.text: In moments of disorganization, reducing variations helps. Fewer stimuli, more support. Fewer choices, more ground.

items.title: Movements with a beginning and an end
items.text: Simple proposals, with clear beginnings and endings, help to build continuity. Knowing when something begins and when it ends restores inner direction.

cap-3.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-3.subtitle: Finding one’s own ground
body: This exercise invites you to perceive, in your own body, how external support organizes what was dispersed.

Approach a firm surface — a wall, the floor, or another person’s body. Rest your hands, feet, or trunk against it. Push gently, feeling the resistance. Stay in that contact for a few seconds. Then step away calmly and observe what has changed inside.

cap-3.text: What organizes when there is support? What settles when something resists alongside?
There is now a place. But knowing where one is differs from knowing where to go. It is from that distinction that movement begins to seek direction. That is where we follow.

cap-4.text: There are situations in which everything seems to happen too quickly.

The space stops responding as before. The passages become confused. What was arriving in sequence begins to arrive together. The body tries to follow, but does not find enough pause to lean on anything.
Something that held the inner movement shifts. The experience loses continuity. The action no longer finds a clear direction to follow.

It is at that point that the crisis sets in. There exists a deep system that holds the sense of being in the world. It organizes the relationship with space, with movement, and with gravity. It is that system that allows one to feel where the body is, where it can go, and when it can stop.

When that organization enters overload, the child does not experience only confusion. An internal sense of instability arises — as if there were not enough support to remain. The body loses reference. Orientation becomes fragile.

Quick transitions, unexpected changes, unstable environments, frequent displacements, and the accumulation of stimuli demand continuous effort to maintain that organization. At certain moments, the body can no longer sustain the rhythm the surroundings impose.

What manifests outwardly — the intense cry, the scream, the sudden rigidity, the disordered movement — is the expression of that state of disorientation. The action arises as an attempt to interrupt the instability, to find a point of support when continuity breaks.

The crisis is born there. As a limit reached. As a survival response. In that state, time loses its contour. The now imposes itself without margin. The inner experience becomes a continuous flow, without clear pauses. The body finds no axis — and the urgency grows because there is still nowhere to land.

It is common for the adult to try to respond with words, explanations, or verbal guidance. But when inner orientation has become fragile, language stops organizing. The body seeks reference before seeking meaning.

The brain prioritizes keeping itself whole. What arrives needs to be held, not interpreted. The child needs something outside herself that offers enough stability for the inner organization to gradually recompose itself.
Slower movements. A stable voice. Predictable gestures. A body that remains when everything around accelerates.
The adult’s presence then becomes a provisional reference point. Not to conduct, not to control — but to hold the space while orientation returns.

The child’s nervous system recognizes that stability. It recognizes the other’s weight. It recognizes a calm that does not react immediately. It recognizes a firmness that does not invade. That is how reorganization begins to happen — by reference, not by imposition.

The crisis does not end all at once. It dissolves gradually. The rhythm decelerates. Breathing finds an interval. The space regains its edges. The body stops falling and begins, little by little, to land.
Then comes the tiredness. A deep tiredness that asks for silence, low demand, and time without expectation. The interior that needed to hold itself together now needs rest.

It is in that interval that trust rebuilds itself. The child learns, without words, that she can become disorganized and be accompanied. That the world can go out of place and someone remains. That losing direction does not mean abandonment.

When the adult recognizes the crisis as a loss of orientation, their own place also adjusts. They stop trying to put out the fire and begin to hold the space. They remain available. They offer time. They wait.
Because when direction is lost, what most orients is someone who knows how to stay.
The crisis does not interrupt the path. It reveals the point where direction became fragile — and where it can be found again.

items.title: Being the rhythm when everything accelerates
items.text: Reduce your own movement. Stabilize your voice. Diminish stimuli. The body organizes itself from what it finds.

items.title: Creating pauses between places
items.text: Before changing environment or activity, offer a brief interval. A few seconds allow the inner orientation to reorganize.

items.title: Offering simple direction
items.text: Few words. Clear gestures. In moments of crisis, a reference point organizes more than an explanation.

items.title: Holding the interval
items.text: Do not rush the return. Orientation reestablishes itself in the body’s time — not the clock’s.

cap-4.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-4.subtitle: Being ground for a moment
body: Stand in silence. Perceive your body before any movement. Notice how it holds itself without conscious effort. Balance happens by itself.
Take a few steps through the space, without choosing direction. Observe how weight transfers, how the body adjusts with each step.
Gradually, slow the rhythm. Allow the movement to find its end. Stop. Feel the weight descend. Feet touching the ground. The body finding rest.

Breathe slowly. Not to calm yourself — but to remain. Hold that sensation. In moments of disorganization, this is what orients before any word: a body that does not accelerate, does not push, and remains available.

cap-4.text: Sometimes, being ground is all the other needs to exist in space again.
When direction returns, the world begins to exist again. But the parts do not always connect immediately. What was lived in fragments now asks for integration. That is where we follow.

cap-5.text: There are moments when the body has found some stability and the world has stopped spinning — and even so, nothing seems to connect. Things happen, but do not form a story. Gestures arise, but do not build continuity. The day goes on, but without clear form.
It is not lack of attention. It is not disinterest. It is another way of receiving the world.

For some children, experience does not arrive as a complete image. It arrives in fragments. An isolated sound. A detail that imposes itself. A gesture without context. A small change that occupies everything. Each piece appears with its own clarity — but does not fit into the whole by itself.
The world does not present itself as a narrative. It presents itself as pieces.

The child perceives the detail before the whole. She feels the smallest variation in the environment before understanding what changed. She grasps the loose gesture before recognizing the intention. She hears the word before perceiving the sentence. She lives the event before being able to connect it to what came before or what will come after.
None of this is an absence of perception. It is an excess of parts without automatic stitching.

While the adult world tends to integrate without effort — joining context, intention, time, and meaning — the child needs to do that work internally, step by step. Each situation demands a silent attempt at connection: what does this have to do with that? Where does this begin? Where does it end? What comes next? It is a continuous effort of inner organization.

When that integration does not happen in time, the world loses meaning. Not because it is empty — but because it arrives loose. Events do not connect. Reactions seem displaced. Responses arise out of time. What, for the observer, seems incoherence, is for the child simply a world received in pieces.

That way of living deeply affects daily life. Simple situations become confusing when there is not enough context. Small changes carry disproportionate weight. Relationships become difficult to sustain when signals do not connect with clarity.

And it is tiring. It is tiring to have to join everything, all the time. It exhausts having to build meaning where it is not offered ready. Living in a world that seems to demand constant translation. Many times, the child withdraws not because she does not want to be there — but because the effort of integrating became too great.

At other times, she fixes on a specific detail — not from rigidity, but because there something can be understood, something that does not escape. When the whole does not form, the detail becomes shelter.
It is at that point that the adult’s presence takes on a silent and decisive function. Not as someone who explains too much, corrects, or accelerates. But as someone who offers connection.

The adult lends meaning to the world when it does not yet organize itself on its own. By naming what is happening. By anticipating what comes next. By connecting beginning, middle, and end. By transforming fragments into simple narrative.

This is not about teaching. It is about stitching. When someone says: “Now we are here. Then we go there. After that, we come back.” When someone connects the gesture to its reason, the situation to its context, the now to what comes next. When someone stays close enough to sustain that connection — something is relieved.
The world does not become less intense. But it becomes more comprehensible.
The child begins to perceive that events relate. That there is a possible sequence. That the parts are not loose forever. That there is a thread — however thin — connecting the experiences.
That thread is not born from within immediately. It is born in the encounter.

Little by little, the child begins to trust that the world can make sense when someone helps to organize it. Not because everything was explained, but because it was lived with coherence. Not because every detail was controlled, but because the whole found form.
When this happens, something fundamental is established: the possibility of integration.
And to integrate is not to understand everything. It is to be able to remain in the world without getting lost in it.

When the parts begin to connect, something finds form. Not because everything became clear — but because it stopped being loose. The world does not need to arrive whole. It only needs to make enough sense for the child to move through it without getting lost.

items.title: Narrating the invisible bridges
items.text: When something changes, say the link that joins the parts. “The water fell — so we are going to get the cloth.” The world stops being a loose fact and becomes a sequence.

items.title: Marking the beginning, the middle, and the end
items.text: Time can also arrive fragmented. In play or tasks, show where something ends. Knowing that there is an edge helps the whole to hold itself.

items.title: The “Yes, and…” technique
items.text: If the focus is on the toy car’s wheel, do not pull away from there. “The wheel spins fast!… and the whole car goes along the road.” The detail is not denied — it is integrated.

items.title: Delivering the map before the territory
items.text: Before a complex scene, present the general picture. “We are going to see people, hear music, and then eat.” When context comes first, the world weighs less.

cap-5.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-5.subtitle: The world through the gap
body: Choose a quiet moment. Make a tube with your hands or use a cardboard roll. Look through it with only one eye.
Walk slowly through the house. Try to do something simple — reaching a door handle, going around a piece of furniture.

Notice how details appear with absolute clarity. And at the same time, how the space around disappears. Feel the insecurity of moving without seeing the whole. Feel the effort of having to guess where you are.
Now stop. Lower the tube. Let your gaze recover the complete space.

cap-5.text: How does the body change when someone describes the path? What would it be like to walk like this every day — seeing pieces, without the whole.
Sometimes, all she needs is someone who says: “We are here. Now we go there.” That is where we follow.

enc-1.text: Perhaps it is not yet possible to explain in words what happened. If someone asked right now, the answer might not come ready. And yet, something has already moved: something has changed in the way of being with the child.

It is not a new technique. It is a different way of remaining. What before felt heavy begins to weigh less. Not because the challenges disappeared — but because the terrain began to be recognized. Certain gestures no longer sound so strange. Certain reactions no longer push so far away.
Not everything becomes comprehensible — and perhaps it never will — but the feeling of being lost no longer occupies the same place.
There is a discreet, almost physical relief in perceiving that it is not about deciphering an enigma — but about inhabiting the same territory. An uneven ground, but now shared.
This changes the quality of care. Presence stops being tense. Being together stops being solitary.

It begins to become clear that many things were not asking for correction. They were asking for company. Asking for time. Asking for someone who stayed close enough to notice how the world arrives there — before demanding any response.
Not total clarity. Proximity. And that proximity awakens a quiet willingness to continue. Not because the path became easy — but because it began to make sense.
There is something deeply human in perceiving that it is not necessary to pull the child into another world. It is possible, gradually, to learn to walk in hers.

The gaze has shifted. The body has found listening. Presence has located itself. The crisis gained a name. The parts began to connect. None of this happened all at once. But it happened. And in happening, it changed the way of being together.
This interval exists for exactly that. So that everything that was read does not transform into theory, nor into demand, nor into hurry. So that it transforms into ground.
Nothing is ready. But something is alive. And when that happens, continuing stops being effort. It becomes the natural gesture of whoever no longer walks alone.

abertura-2.subtitle:
WHEN FEELING IS NOT ENOUGH
Action in the world

abertura-2.text: In the first part of this book, the invitation was to learn to remain. To adjust the gaze. To recognize what happens internally before any action becomes possible. There, the focus was on experience. On the feeling that precedes the gesture. On the body that needs to find ground before responding to the world.

But there is a moment when that is no longer enough. There is a point where the child feels, perceives, recognizes — and yet cannot act. Or acts for a moment, but does not hold. Or begins, but gets lost in the middle. Or even does it, but at too high a cost.
It is there that this part begins. Part II does not abandon what was built before. It rests on it. But it shifts the field.
Here, the focus becomes the doing — not as external demand, nor as expected performance, but as something that needs to be organized to become possible.

To act is not a simple gesture. It demands initiating, sustaining, directing, finishing. It demands moving through transitions, dealing with choices, maintaining attention, tolerating effort. It demands, many times, something that is not yet available internally.
That is why, in this part, the adult’s presence becomes more active. Not to do it for the child. Not to push. But to lend structure.
Structure of time. Structure of space. Structure of language. Structure of meaning.

Everything that appears here is born from daily life. From the home. From simple tasks. From the small actions that repeat every day and, precisely because of that, reveal where the doing gets lost — and where it can be held.

Throughout the next chapters, it becomes evident that action rarely fails for a single reason. Sometimes, the impasse is at the beginning. At other times, in the middle. There are cases where it arises from excess stimulus, from lack of rhythm, from the absence of direction or of meaning.
None of this happens in isolation. None of this resolves with a single strategy.
What is built here is a field of reading. A way of perceiving where to enter, when to hold, when to delimit, when to orient with words, when to organize the day, when to use interest as a bridge.

Part II does not propose control. It proposes conditions. Conditions for action to stop depending exclusively on another’s effort and begin, little by little, to organize itself from inside to outside — always in relationship.
If Part I was about inhabiting the world internally, Part II is about making it possible to inhabit the world in action.
Not as a straight line. Not as constant progress. But as living, adjusted, real construction. That is where we follow.

cap-6.text: With time, it becomes possible to observe better. Signals begin to be recognized, limits anticipated, rhythm adjusted. The child’s body no longer seems like an unknown territory; there is less alarm, less urgency. A kind of ground begins to form.

And yet, something remains. The day goes on. The requests are simple, the situations already known, and the child is there — present, attentive. Even so, there are moments when the action does not begin. Not as a crisis. Not as refusal. Only as a delay difficult to name.
That interval draws attention precisely because, from outside, everything seems ready.

The space between perceiving and acting always existed, but now becomes more visible. Perhaps because the body is more regulated. Perhaps because the environment is more predictable. Or because, for the first time, what is missing is not containing the feeling — but sustaining the beginning.
There is an important difference between not being able to do and not being able to begin.

Many children follow well when something is already in progress. The challenge appears earlier, at the source of the movement, at the first step. That is where the body hesitates. Like someone holding the key in front of the right door, knowing exactly where to go, but unable to turn it. Or like the child who already has the coat in her hands, ready to leave, but cannot pass her arm through the first sleeve.

Waiting, rarely, crosses that point. Internally, that pause is inhabited. The body works silently. It tries to organize how to enter, where to lean, how to begin the movement. The intention exists. The understanding too.
But the action has not yet found enough support to arise. The more the beginning weighs, the more difficult it becomes to cross alone.

It is common, at that moment, for the request to be repeated, for the explanation to come again, or for silence to be maintained in the expectation that clarity will make the movement appear. Sometimes it works. Many times, it does not.

Because what is missing there is no longer explanation. The child’s body has already understood what comes next. What has not yet formed is a support point for beginning. Where to place the body. How to enter the action. How to take the first step without everything weighing at once.
When that support does not yet exist internally, it can be offered from outside.
To lend the beginning is not to do it for the child. Not to lead the whole path, nor to accelerate. It is to enter exactly where the weight is greatest: at the first step.

Sometimes this happens in a minimal movement. The adult holds the coat together, helps to pass the first sleeve, and stops. Or holds the sheet while the first stroke happens. Or stands up together, only so that the child’s body finds the initial impulse.

The action is not resolved; it is unlocked. When the beginning is shared, something changes. The child’s body stops carrying alone the effort of starting. The weight distributes. The movement finds support. And from there, it can continue.

That support is temporary. It enters at the beginning and withdraws when the action holds. It does not create dependency; it creates experience. The body learns, little by little, that it is possible to cross that point.

There is also something that reorganizes in the adult. It becomes clearer that it is not necessary to push, to insist, or to explain more. Care changes place when one recognizes that the function there is not to demand will — but to offer base. Not to wait passively, nor to control the path — it is to give ground to the beginning until the movement organizes itself.

Beginning is not simple. And it does not need to be solitary. For some children, the greatest effort is not in doing — but in crossing the first step. When the beginning finds support, the path stops being an obstacle and becomes a possible process.

items.title: Observe where the movement gets stuck. Notice the exact moment when the child seems ready — but does not advance. Not the after. Not the end. Only that suspended point.
When nothing happens, observe where tension arises. In the chest. In the shoulders. That sensation usually indicates that the beginning is too heavy to cross alone.
Ask yourself whether the situation asks for more words or a first shared movement.
items.text: Leaving as soon as the action sustains itself

cap-6.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-6.subtitle: The weight of the first step
body: Choose something simple from the day. Something whose way of doing it is already known. Before beginning, pause. Stay a few seconds with the intention clear, without acting.
Then imagine someone beginning together: holding the door, taking the first step, sharing the initial weight. Notice the difference.
Many times, that is exactly where the child is.

cap-6.text: Sometimes what seems like hesitation is only a body trying to find how to enter. Not every delay is resistance. Not every lateness is lack of understanding. There are beginnings that ask for more than intention. They ask for enough support for the first step to exist without weighing too much.

When the beginning finds enough support, action becomes possible. But beginning does not yet guarantee that the movement will hold itself. The gesture is born, but does not hold. It is at that point that care needs to change place. That is where we follow.

cap-7.text: After the beginning becomes possible, a new kind of challenge begins to appear. The gesture is born, the action takes shape, the child enters the doing. There is no more immobility, nor absence. Something has effectively begun to move.

And yet, that movement does not hold. The beginning happens, but comes undone too soon. The action arises, but does not find enough continuity to go on. This is not refusal, nor crisis. It is a doing that enters the scene — but does not remain.
It is on that unstable terrain that the adult’s presence needs to reorganize itself.

The first movement happens. From outside, everything indicates that the activity has begun. Shortly after, something is lost. The action does not interrupt itself abruptly; it simply does not sustain itself. What already became possible does not transform into a path.

That instant is usually perceived with clarity by whoever accompanies. The child begins something. The gesture is born. The beginning has already happened. Almost at the same time, however, the movement pulls away. What has not yet established itself is the continuing.

In daily life, this appears in a simple way. The child sits down to draw, to build something, or to organize toys. She begins. She makes a first movement. For a moment, everything seems on track. Then she stands up, looks around, lets herself be captured by another stimulus.
There is no opposition. There is no explosion. Only a loss of continuity.
The adult calls back. Helps to resume. The beginning happens again. Shortly after, the same movement repeats itself. The entry exists, but dissolves too soon.

Here it is important to name precisely what is happening. When the beginning needs to be re-lent repeatedly, the difficulty is no longer in the beginning. It is in the middle. More specifically, in the lack of enough support for the action to sustain itself over time.

Each stretch of doing demands a new inner organization. Each small advance asks for a reconquest of focus, of axis, of direction. The child can recognize the activity, understand what she is doing, and even be interested in it. What is not yet available is the possibility of maintaining the path without needing to reconstruct it at every few steps.
The first gesture is possible, but the next one is not yet guaranteed. The action happens, but does not chain itself. Sustaining is missing.

Faced with this, it is common for the adult to insist on the beginning. That seems logical, because it was like that that the movement arose for the first time. But when the difficulty is in sustaining, insisting on the beginning does not resolve it. It only reinforces the dependence on the restart.
It is here that the adult’s function needs to change place. If before it was necessary to lend the beginning, now it becomes necessary to hold the middle.

That change does not happen by trial and error. It begins with observation. Instead of asking “how do I make a start happen again?”, the gaze shifts: where exactly does this path lose support? At what point does the action come undone? How long can it hold before dissolving?

That reading happens in daily life, in real time. At the table, when the drawing stops in the middle. In the bedroom, when the child begins to dress and disperses before finishing. In the transitions of the day, when one step is taken but the next does not come.
This is not about surveilling more, nor about controlling better. It is about seeing with precision.
When the point where the action comes undone becomes visible, the adult’s positioning changes. The gesture stops being to initiate and becomes to sustain.

To sustain is not to do it for the child. It is to become an anchoring presence. It is to remain in the space of the activity long enough so that the path does not need to be reconstructed from zero every time.

In practice, this can mean being closer at that specific stretch — without speaking more, without explaining more, without conducting. In certain moments, sustaining passes through simplifying the surroundings: reducing what distracts, diminishing what competes, clarifying the point where the action usually gets lost.

Sustaining with presence, not with words. In the home, this can be as simple as sitting alongside for a few more minutes during the activity. Or remaining present during tidying up, without taking over the task — but also without disappearing.
On outings, it can mean adjusting the family’s rhythm. Accompanying the play for longer. Staying together on the path, instead of only starting it and waiting for her to continue alone.
That gesture is not conducting. Not rescuing. It is holding the space.

When the adult positions themselves this way, something begins to change. The action does not become stable all at once. It does not hold for long periods. But it lasts a little longer. The path firms itself for a few moments beyond the usual.

And that is already significant. Continuity is not built with explanation. It is built with experience. Each time the child lives a doing that sustains itself a little longer, something organizes internally. The path begins to be recognized. The action stops depending exclusively on the borrowed initial impulse.
This chapter does not offer a ready technique. It offers a criterion.

When the beginning happens but does not hold, the intervention stops being at the beginning and starts to inhabit the middle. That displacement does not resolve everything, but creates the conditions for the next step to become possible.
For some children, the challenge is not entering the action. It is remaining in it long enough for the path to exist.

items.title: Observe a daily activity. Not the beginning. Not the end. Only the exact point where the action usually comes undone. Stay there for a few moments, in silence, without intervening immediately.

At the next interruption, notice the impulse to call to begin again. See if it is possible, before that, to remain together exactly where the action stopped — without speaking, without explaining, only sustaining presence.
During a simple activity, try inhabiting the space of the task for longer. Do not do it for the child. Do not anticipate. Stay in the middle of the path with her.

cap-7.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-7.subtitle: The middle of the path
body: Choose a simple activity from your day and begin. After a few moments, stop in the middle. Observe the impulse to restart from zero. The discomfort of remaining without concluding. The urge to jump to the end.
Now, resume from exactly where you stopped. Without restarting. Only continue.
Notice the difference between restarting and sustaining the middle. Many times, that is exactly where the child is.

cap-7.text: There are gestures that do not fall for lack of will — but for lack of ground in the middle of the path. To sustain is not to rush. Not to conduct. It is to remain close enough so that the doing does not need to disappear in order to restart.
When the action begins to firm itself, even if for a short time, another need appears. The doing asks for contour. Clear limits. A field that helps the path not to spread. That is where we follow.

cap-8.text: After the beginning becomes possible and the middle begins to hold, another challenge begins to reveal itself. The child has impulse, interest, and energy to act. The movement is born. The doing announces itself. And yet — it does not fix itself.
The action spreads. The gesture touches many things, passes through different objects and invitations, but stays in none of them — as if the energy opened too early, before finding form.
Before thinking about what the child does, it is worth observing where this happens.

The space, many times, is full. Objects in view, open possibilities, stimuli that offer themselves at the same time. The environment keeps speaking, even when no one says anything, calling to many places at once.
In that scene, the child moves. She touches, begins, explores. There is interest. There is enough energy to act.
And yet, the doing does not find form. Not because something is missing — but because there is too much.
This chapter approaches that specific territory: when action exists, but needs edges not to spread. When the gesture asks for less opening and more definition in order to continue.

In daily life, this tends to appear in a silent way. The home is in movement. Accessible toys, scattered materials, objects in view even when not in use. Nothing is out of place. Everything is available.
The child circulates. Approaches one thing, then another. The gesture continues — but does not deepen. There is enough action to fill the time, but not enough to sustain a path.
When observed carefully, it becomes clear that this is not lack of interest. The child is in movement, trying to manage a field too wide to organize alone.

The challenge is not in acting — it is in choosing where to stay. It is like being in a place where all the doors are open at the same time. Each one calls. Each one promises something. None closes enough for the next step to find support.

Without edges, the action does not fall. It distributes itself. The doing happens — but does not gain weight. It does not create the sense of a path. It does not leave a trace. And without that experience, everything remains in a state of attempt.
It is at that point that the adult’s positioning reorganizes itself again.
After helping to begin and sustaining the middle, it becomes necessary to delimit the field of action. Not to reduce the child’s world — but to make it inhabitable.
Creating edges is offering a possible contour. It is saying, without many words: this is where we are now; this is what belongs to this moment; it goes up to here.
Those edges are not long rules or rigid structures. They are simple, visible, temporary contours. They enter as external support while the child cannot yet sustain that limit internally.
In the home, this can happen concretely. Fewer objects available at a time. A chosen space for the activity. A beginning lived together and a recognized ending — even if brief.
When the field is defined, something changes. The action gains density. The gesture finds where to land.
With fewer competing paths, the path strengthens. The child can remain for longer because she does not need to decide every instant where to go. Energy stops dispersing and begins to concentrate.

To delimit does not impoverish the experience. It gives it form. Within a clearer space, the doing repeats. Attention settles. The gesture deepens. Something can be lived until the end — even in a simple way. And that lived experience matters.
The edges do not enter permanently. They appear as support while the internal contour is still forming.
Gradually, they can be loosened, widened, or removed. Not by external decision — but because the child begins to recognize when an action begins, when it is in progress, and when it can end.

Not as a taught rule. As a repeated experience. That is how action stops spreading. And begins to organize itself. For some children, acting is not difficult. What is difficult is remaining when everything calls at the same time. Edges do not limit movement. They offer ground.

items.title: Observe the space where the child usually acts. See if there are too many possibilities open at the same time. Try reducing — not to control, but to clarify.
Before starting an activity, help to define where it will happen. A recognizable space helps the gesture to sustain itself.
During a simple action, stay present until the ending. Not to conduct — but to hold the contour from beginning to end.

cap-8.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-8.subtitle: The field of one’s own doing
body: Choose a simple activity from your day. Before beginning, observe the environment around you. How many things compete for attention? What could be set aside for a few minutes?
Now perform the action in a smaller field. Notice the difference. Many times, that is exactly what the child needs.

cap-8.text: There are gestures that get lost not for lack of energy — but for excess of possibilities. When the space is defined, the action finds where to stay.

When the space of the action becomes clearer, another possibility begins to arise. The word starts to enter as support — not to explain too much, but to help the doing to sustain itself. That is where we follow.

cap-9.text: After action finds beginning, middle, and contour, another element begins to gain relevance. The doing is happening. The child enters activities, remains a little longer. The space helps; presence holds.
And yet, in many moments, the movement seems to follow without a clear point of orientation — as if something were missing that helps to locate the doing while it happens.

It is at that point that the word begins to carry another weight. It stops functioning only as accompaniment and begins to act as a brief reference. A word that points. That cuts. That helps to locate the doing when many possibilities offer themselves at the same time.

When the space already has edges — chosen objects, delimited field, clearer surroundings — the word enters to organize what happens within that field. It does not replace the physical contour; it orients the movement that has already found where to stay.
This tends to appear simply in daily life. A “here.” A “now.” A “done.”
Short words — that do not resolve the action by themselves, but offer enough direction for it to remain alive and organized for longer.

When action happens without direction, it tends to spread. The child moves, touches, begins different parts of the same activity. There is energy. There is interest. What appears is the difficulty of choosing a point within the doing to stay.

That experience arises in common situations. In the living room, when various toys call at the same time. During a simple task, when one part begins before the previous one has ended. In displacements, when the body moves but still searches for a clear place within what is being done.

Faced with this, it is frequent for the adult to try to help by expanding the speech. The intention is to offer clarity. However, when many words enter together, the field tends to open even further, demanding an additional organization effort.

Here, the adjustment follows another direction. Less quantity. More precision. At that stage of development, the word acts as a verbal gesture. It does not explain the whole path — it indicates where to step now.
When it fulfills that function, the word works as a minimal compass. It does not draw long maps. It helps to maintain direction while the movement happens.
Some words become especially effective because they fit inside the doing. They do not ask for elaboration or anticipation. They only ask for recognition.
The child does not need to understand everything involved in the task. She needs to be able to locate herself within it.
That word does not organize the action alone. It creates a passage. It opens a brief interval of clarity within the movement in progress.

With time, it becomes perceptible that the child’s response changes when the word appears at the right moment. Not before — preparing too much. Not after — when the action has already dispersed. But alongside the doing, holding the point where it is possible to stay.
The word does not lead the whole path. It accompanies the immediate stretch. It does not replace experience; it helps the child to remain within it.

At that stage, language begins to fulfill a new function: marking places in time and space of the doing. Some words begin to be recognized as stable references. They stop sounding like noise and begin to function as signals that organize.

That process happens gradually. The word needs to be lived many times in the same type of situation to gain meaning. Not as a formal rule — but as a repeated experience that inscribes itself in the body and in memory.
What is built here is not mastery of language — it is familiarity with words that help action find its direction.

This chapter invites the observation of when the word supports the doing — and when it occupies too much space. The difference tends to lie less in content and more in the moment and the way it enters.
Sometimes, a single well-placed word holds more than a whole explanation.
When the word points to a possible place, the doing finds direction — and the movement follows with more clarity.

cap-9.title: SMALL PRACTICES
cap-9.subtitle: Choosing one word at a time

items.title: In a simple activity, observe which word helps the child to locate herself in that moment. Use only that word while the doing is in progress.
Say the word while the doing is in progress. Observe whether that favors remaining and reduces dispersion.
When many possibilities open up at the same time, use the word to indicate one place: where to stay, what to touch, which part to sustain now.

cap-9.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-9.subtitle: The word that orients
body: During an activity from your day, observe how many words you usually use to orient yourself. In another moment, repeat the same action using only one short word as reference.
Notice the difference between explaining the path and indicating one point. Between speaking to organize — and speaking to orient.
Many times, that is the same difference the child also needs to experience.

cap-9.text: Some words do not teach — they indicate where to stay. When language finds that place, it stops occupying space and starts opening a path.
When the word begins to offer direction, time asks for organization. It is in rhythm, in repetition, and in predictability that the doing finds continuity. That is where we follow.

cap-10.text: After the word begins to offer direction, another element begins to sustain the doing throughout the day. Time stops being only a succession of moments and begins to gain form.
The day begins. The home sets in motion. The child moves between spaces, objects, and small actions. When the day’s sequence is recognizable, something organizes itself before any request is made.

The doing finds support before being called. With time, it becomes perceptible that when the day follows a known order, daily experience demands less effort. The child does not need to guess what comes next. The path has already been lived. The action finds support before even beginning.

That is rhythm. In the home, that rhythm appears in a simple way. In the morning that repeats. In the departure that always happens in the same order. In the end of the day that returns to familiar gestures.

At that point, routine stops being only external organization. It begins to function as daily ground — a ground that removes from the child the need to decide all the time. A ground that saves energy for what really matters.
When every moment of the day needs to be reinvented, experience remains on alert. One must remember what to do, choose where to go, sustain continuous attention.
When a predictable sequence exists, part of that work is sustained by the environment. The day becomes lighter because it stops demanding constant vigilance.

Repetition, here, does not impoverish. Repetition strengthens. The same path, lived many times, creates familiarity. Familiarity opens space for the action to sustain itself. The gesture happens with less tension. Transitions stop being fragile points. The day begins to find its own form.
It is in that context that visual support takes on a central role. Not as a technique, but as a natural extension of rhythm.

For many children, seeing organizes more stably than hearing. The visual remains available. It does not demand active memory. It does not depend on the constant presence of the adult. A signal in the space, a visible order, a simple support that indicates what comes next.
The visual anticipates time and sustains the continuity of the doing.

When the next step is visible, the child follows with more safety. The action finds support because time stops being a constant surprise. The rhythm holds without needing to be explained every instant.
In daily life, this appears in simple forms. A separated object that marks the next stage. An image that signals the transition. A fixed order that repeats every day.

Nothing sophisticated. Only enough to make the day legible. That kind of support does not replace the relationship — it extends it. When the adult does not need to speak all the time, the environment sustains. The visual carries the rhythm when words have already tired. It remains there, in silence, offering continuity.

With time, something important happens. The child begins to recognize patterns. The day no longer starts from zero. Yesterday’s lived path leaves traces. The known sequence sustains the next one. Action begins to chain itself with less effort.

Each organized day leaves something for the following one. This is not about automating life — it is about creating enough base so that the new can arise without disorganizing everything. Routine, when alive and adjusted, does not limit. It offers contour. Within that contour, the child experiments, creates, explores.
The adult’s role here is clear. Choosing what repeats. Sustaining the form of the day. Adjusting when necessary — without dismantling everything at every variation.
That demands intention, presence, and reading of the moment. It demands perceiving when sustaining matters more than changing.

When rhythm is established, the day stops being a collection of loose demands. It becomes a recognizable sequence. The child begins to anticipate. The doing organizes itself with less direct support. Action gains continuity.
Routine does not teach on its own. It creates the space where learning becomes possible.
For many children, the greatest effort is not in the task. It is in the day that has not yet organized itself. When rhythm is established, the doing finds its path.

items.title: Observe at which moments of the day the child needs more effort to act. Notice the transition, the before and after — not only the task itself.
Choose a daily sequence and sustain it for a few days. Repetition helps to recognize the path without depending on constant explanation.
Whenever possible, make what comes next visible. A separated object, a signal in the space, or a simple image helps to sustain continuity.

cap-10.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-10.subtitle: Feeling the rhythm of the day
body: Choose a moment of the day that usually happens always in the same way. Move through that sequence with attention. Notice how the gestures anticipate themselves without much thought.
Now imagine that same moment happening in an unpredictable way. Observe the difference in the effort required.
Many times, that is the additional effort the child lives when the day has not yet found its form.

cap-10.text: When the day has form, action finds support before even happening. Predictability holds movement and allows it to continue.
When the day finds rhythm and predictability, another force begins to orient the doing. Personal interest starts to give meaning to the path and to sustain engagement. That is where we follow.

cap-11.text: After the day finds rhythm, action finds contour, and the word begins to orient the path, something begins to stand out more clearly. Not everything sustains itself in the same way. Some tasks flow with ease. Others demand effort, negotiation, repetition — not because they are more difficult in themselves, but because they do not carry enough meaning to maintain the doing.

It is at that point that interest enters the field. Not as a sophisticated strategy, nor as a resource external to daily life. Interest appears as what, in practice, has always moved the child. It is the force that pulls the gesture when the task alone does not carry enough weight to sustain the action.

In daily life, this reveals itself simply. Storing the toy does not awaken desire. Putting on the coat does not draw attention. Tying the shoe does not offer immediate meaning. Riding the bicycle, yes. Watching the favorite video, yes. Playing with something that awakens curiosity, yes.

When interest enters the field, the path begins to organize itself. First this. Then that. Not as imposition — but as a comprehensible direction. The child is not being deceived. She is being oriented by something that makes sense to her. Interest functions as traction: it does not erase the difficulty, but creates a reason to cross it.
When interest becomes a concrete horizon, the quality of action changes. The body organizes itself with less resistance. The doing finds an immediate why.
Storing the toy stops being only a demand. It becomes the path to something desired.

That use of interest is not bargaining. It is not a coin invented to manipulate behavior. It is the recognition of a force that already exists in the child — only positioned in a way that sustains the path to it.

The difference between interest and reward lies in origin. Interest comes from the child: it is what she seeks, what moves her, what makes her eyes light up. Reward comes from outside: it is something chosen by the adult to modify behavior. Interest was already there. Reward is introduced.
When interest is used as support, dependence on external prizes is not created. What is already important is recognized — and a path is built that makes sense for the child to cross.

Beyond daily tasks, interest also organizes the pedagogical field. A child interested in animals draws more easily when the theme involves animals. A child who loves cars engages more when numbers, colors, or stories pass through that world.

Interest creates narrative. And narrative sustains presence. In that movement, the adult does not force learning. They offer content by the path the child already travels. Interest is not the final objective. It is the contour that allows the task to exist.

Used that way, interest stops being something isolated and begins to structure daily life. It sustains less desired tasks. It organizes activities. It creates continuity between what the child loves and what needs to be done.

This chapter does not propose making the child enjoy everything. It proposes recognizing that not everything sustains itself on its own — and that interest is one of the most potent forces for giving direction to the doing.

Using interest, however, demands adjustment. It needs to be clear, concrete, and achievable. Vague promises do not sustain action. Interest needs to be in sight, fitting within the child’s sense of time.
“After this, we go riding bikes.” “After, you can play with that.” “After, we watch together.”
The “after” cannot be too distant. It needs to be close enough to keep the path alive.
Well positioned, interest does not dominate the day. It organizes passages. The task happens. The interest comes. The cycle closes.
With time, something important is built. The child begins to recognize the logic of the path. Not as an abstract rule — but as a lived experience.
There are things that are crossed to reach others. There are paths that make sense because they lead to something desired.
That is the construction of function — without needing to be named.
Interest stops being only a reward and begins to function as an axis of daily life organization. It sustains routines. It anchors tasks. It creates real engagement.

This chapter does not close Part II by offering a final technique. It widens the field. It shows that, between rhythm, edge, word, and sequence, there exists something that crosses everything: what makes sense to the child.
Interest does not resolve everything. But without it, many actions simply do not happen.
When interest is recognized, respected, and well positioned, the doing gains direction. Daily life stops being only demand and becomes a possible path.
For many children, the challenge is not knowing how to do. It is having a reason to do. When interest enters the field, effort finds meaning and action finds direction.

items.title: Notice what the child seeks spontaneously. What makes her remain, ask for more, repeat. That is the starting point.
In less desired tasks, make explicit what comes next. Short, concrete, and possible.
Whenever possible, incorporate themes of interest in the activities of the day: drawings, stories, organization, conversations.

cap-11.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-11.subtitle: Feeling what motivates
body: Think of a task from the day that you usually avoid. Then think of something desired right after. Observe how the body organizes itself when there is a clear reason to cross what weighs.
Many times, that is exactly what the child needs: not less demand, but more meaning.

cap-11.text: There are actions that only exist when something pulls them. Interest does not simplify the path — but offers a reason to cross it.
Now that we have moved through the elements that sustain the doing, it becomes possible to integrate them. That is where we follow, in the Closing of Part II.

enc-2.text: Throughout this part, something has been becoming clear, even without needing to be said directly: to act is not an isolated gesture. It is a process that builds itself. It does not begin only when the child understands. It does not sustain itself only because it had a start. It does not hold only by will. Acting needs ground. Needs contour. Needs direction, rhythm, language, and meaning.

Each chapter moved through one point of that path — not as rigid stages, but as layers that overlap in real life. On some days, what weighs is the beginning. On others, it is the middle. On others, the excess of stimulus, the lack of rhythm, or the absence of meaning.
None of this happens in a straight line. What is built here is a form of looking. A way of perceiving where the doing gets lost — and where it can be held.

When the adult lends the beginning, action finds its entry. When they sustain the middle, it gains permanence. When they offer edges, the gesture does not spread. When they use words that orient, movement finds direction. When the day gains rhythm, the body saves effort. When interest enters the scene, the doing finds reason.

These supports do not execute the action in the child’s place. They create conditions for action to exist, to hold, and, little by little, to organize itself from inside to outside — always in relationship.

Part II does not offer quick solutions. It offers a living structure. A structure that is born in the relationship, rests on daily life, and adjusts to the child who exists — with her time, her strengths, and her real limits.
At the end of this path, something can begin to change in daily life. Not because everything became simple — but because the doing began to be more legible.
It becomes possible to recognize where to enter. Where to remain. Where to delimit. Where to orient. Where to repeat. Where to use interest as a bridge.
Acting stops being only constant demand and becomes a possible field. It is from that field that the next movement can happen.

abertura-3.subtitle:
WHEN THE WORLD STOPS RESPONDING THE SAME WAY
The other as presence that asks for mediation

abertura-3.text: Until here, something was organizing itself. The child already acts with more intention. The doing finds support. The day gains form. Words, rhythms, and interests help to sustain the path.
The functioning, in great part, depends on the body itself, on the prepared environment, and on the references that repeat. The acting happens. Daily life continues.

Then, something changes in nature. It is not the world that transforms. It is someone who appears. A presence begins to occupy the space of the doing. Not as a bond, not as a relationship to be understood — but as a factor that interferes. Someone who enters the field of action and alters the conditions for it to continue happening.
The gesture that before followed needs to adjust. Time no longer responds only to its own rhythm. The path encounters interruptions, detours, waits that were not planned.

This is not yet about the other as a social encounter. It is about the other as a presence that demands mediation. A functional obstacle that forces the doing to reorganize itself so as not to come apart.
The child is not trying to understand anyone. She is trying to make things work.

It is in that territory that this part of the book moves. Here, development does not advance by the acquisition of new abilities, but by the necessity of sustaining action when the previous guarantees are no longer enough on their own. The body needs to tolerate detours. The action needs to remain even when it does not respond immediately. Time needs to be endured.

Meanwhile, something also shifts from outside. The adult, who until here organized, anticipated, and sustained the functioning, begins to occupy another place. Not as trainer. Not as specialist. But as an axis capable of reading impasses, sustaining interruptions, and mediating paths when the doing encounters resistance.
This part of the book does not promise linearity. It does not transform difficulty into deficit. It does not rush the entry into social relationship.
It accompanies — with precision and respect — the point where acting stops being sufficient and remaining becomes necessary.
It is exactly there that something new can begin to be built.

When action encounters resistance, the immediate impulse tends to be to retreat or to break. But there exists another possibility: sustaining the interval without abandoning the doing. That is where we follow, in Chapter 12.

cap-12.text: There is a moment when something becomes evident in daily life.
The child wants something. Wants it now. Wants to touch. Wants to reach. Wants to continue.

The body orients itself toward the object, toward the action, toward what awakens interest. The intention appears in the gesture that advances, in the gaze that fixes, in the movement that approaches.

What is not yet available is a simple means for crossing the distance between wanting and reaching. The interest exists. The direction too. Missing is a short path that connects one thing to the other.
It is at that point that the word begins to take on another place. As concrete support for the action to happen.
In daily life, this appears simply. The child extends her hand. Approaches. Tries to take. The object is there. The desire too.
When a short word enters joined to the gesture — at the right time, linked to what is being lived — something organizes.
The word does not replace the gesture. It accompanies it. A brief sound. Recognizable. Always the same. Something that can be repeated. Something that points to what is at stake in that instant.
With repetition, the body begins to associate. The gesture starts to carry a new support. The child perceives that that sound has an effect. That it opens a path. That it makes the world respond.

At that moment, the word functions as a practical resource. It connects intention to action. It connects interest to achievement. It connects the child to the world in a direct and possible way. The quality of the relationship changes. The word stops being only sound and begins to operate in the field of doing.
In small and repeated experiences, this becomes visible. The child wants to play with something specific. Wants to continue an activity. Wants to leave. Wants to repeat.

When the word always arises associated with the same action, at the same point of the path, it begins to gain functional meaning. The child learns that that sound has a consequence. That using it brings closer. That it helps to reach something real. Interest sustains the effort of using the word because the response comes right after.
That is a fundamental point: the word needs to work. When it works, the child uses it. When it does not work, it gets lost.
That is why, at this beginning, language builds itself joined to interest. What the child desires is the engine that maintains the use. The word enters as a key that turns.

With time, something begins to happen. The child begins to anticipate. She no longer needs only to extend her hand. The word begins to appear before the complete gesture. It arises as a resource for organizing the action.

The relationship gains a new axis. The child begins to mark presence in another way. The interest, that before expressed itself only through gesture, begins to have a sound support that accompanies it.
That use of the word does not ask for hurry. It asks for consistency. The same word. The same meaning. The same response.
When that holds, the child begins to trust that path. Language stops being loose effort and begins to integrate daily doing.
Gradually, the field widens. The word that before served only to reach something starts to accompany small actions: storing, opening, closing, continuing, stopping.
Always connected to what is happening. Always anchored in the present.
Here the base establishes itself. The word shows its value in action before serving as an instrument of exchange.
It organizes the doing, sustains interest, and produces a concrete effect in the world.
When the child discovers that she can use language to act in the world, something opens. The word stops being a loose sound and becomes a means of passage.

items.title: Notice what the child seeks frequently, where the gesture orients, what she tries to reach repeatedly.
Use short words, always linked to the same action. Less variation, more clarity.
When the word appears, the response comes. Predictability sustains the use.
items.text: Avoiding expanding before the right time

cap-12.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-12.subtitle: Feeling when the word works
body: Think of something simple from daily life that requires a specific means to give access: a code, a command, a brief request. Notice how the body organizes itself when that means works.
Now imagine not having access to it. For the child, the word begins exactly there: as a means that opens — or closes — paths.

cap-12.text: Language is not born to explain the world. It is born to allow access to it.

When the word begins to function as a means for reaching, something new begins to happen in the field of action. The world stops responding only to direct gesture, and the other’s presence begins to interfere in that path. That is where we follow.
