cap-13.text: At a certain point in development, the word no longer serves only to reach something outside. It begins to approach what happens internally. The child already uses words to ask, to continue, to stop, to choose. Language functions as support for action and produces a concrete effect in the world. That use is already established. What begins to transform now is the place where the word acts.
Experience stops being only external. Something of what happens internally begins to ask for a mark.

It is recognition. The child lives distinct states — tiredness, excitement, frustration, expectation — and begins to need a means for signaling those variations without depending only on gesture or physical intensity.

That movement appears in daily life in a very concrete way. The activity loses rhythm. The child withdraws. The action interrupts itself without apparent reason. Or, on the contrary, excitement grows and finds no contour. What changes is not the external situation — but the internal state.

It is at that point that the adult begins to occupy a decisive place. Not to interpret, nor to explain what the child feels — but to name with enough precision what is already being lived. A simple word, short, repeated always in the same type of situation, enters joined to the experience.
“Tired.” “Enough.” “Upset.” “More.” Those words function as initial marks of inner states. They give contour to what before remained only dispersed, without recognizable form.

When the adult names this way — at the right time, without expanding, without lecturing — something organizes. The child begins to perceive that what happens internally can be identified. That there are variations that can be recognized and sustained.

Emotion, here, is something to be located. That recognition changes the quality of the relationship. The adult stops needing to guess constantly. The child begins to signal, remaining in contact with her own experience as it happens.
The word begins to function as an inner marker that finds a response in the environment.
When this repeats itself, a circuit begins to form: something happens internally → someone names it → the environment adjusts.

The child learns, through experience, that what she feels can be recognized — and that that recognition produces an effect. The rhythm changes. The demand diminishes. The activity ends. The play continues. The limit is respected.

By coherent response. That is how the named emotion begins to be part of development. The child starts to differentiate states, to recognize transitions, to perceive that the day is not one single block. The inner contour strengthens.

Gradually, something broader prepares itself. When the child recognizes what happens inside, she also begins to notice that the other responds to that. The other’s presence stops being only functional and begins to be perceived as part of the field — as someone who adjusts, holds, and responds.
That is a sensitive point of development. It asks for consistent repetition and stable presence. The adult names, sustains, and responds — without expanding beyond what is necessary.
Feeling needs to have a name before the conversation about feelings. Inner recognition needs to exist before the understanding of the other.
When the word begins to give form to inner experience, the shared field becomes possible.

items.title: Notice when the child’s rhythm alters throughout the day. Those moments ask for simple naming.
Choose few words for frequent states and repeat them always in the same type of situation.
When the word appears, the environment adjusts. The response sustains the use.

cap-13.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-13.subtitle: When something is recognized
body: Think of a moment when someone perceived your tiredness, your tension, or your need for pause — and adjusted the rhythm without explaining, without advising.
Notice the effect of that. For the child, the word begins exactly like that: as recognition that organizes what was dispersed.

cap-13.text: To name is not to explain. It is to allow what happens internally to find enough form not to overflow.

When inner experience begins to gain contour and recognition, something new becomes possible: the child can begin to remain regulated when the environment changes — including when that environment is another body. The next movement begins here.

cap-14.text: Until here, the world responded in a relatively predictable way. Objects were available. Routines repeated themselves. Words helped to organize the doing. Action found support and followed.

When the child begins to recognize what she feels internally, something new becomes possible: remaining regulated when the environment changes — including when that environment is another body. She manages to hold herself a little better when it appears.

At a certain moment, something changes. The space is no longer occupied only by one’s own intention. Someone crosses the path. A hand arrives first. A sound invades. A different rhythm imposes itself. The environment, which before seemed neutral, begins to be shared.

The other enters the scene. At first, as a concrete presence. This reveals itself in simple daily situations. Two children approach the same toy. A game demands alternation. The corridor is too narrow when two run at the same time. The action that was flowing encounters an unexpected limit.
It is a raw encounter. The child feels the impact. The gesture that worked alone now stumbles into something. There is another will at play. The world no longer responds only to her movement.

At that point, something delicate installs itself. The child does not necessarily yet have the notion that the other can be hurt. The impulse arrives whole. The force enters completely. The intention is to continue — not to hurt. But the effect can be excessive.
There is a brief moment — tense, visible — in which the action freezes. The hand stops in the air. The movement stiffens. The gaze searches for reference. The gesture loses continuity.
That interval is precious. The adult, here, does not abandon. Nor does she take control. The adult holds the space.
She is there. Present. Attentive. Close enough to guarantee safety. Distant enough not to steal the experience. The adult’s presence signals a limit without crushing the movement.
She does not rush. Does not moralize. Does not transform the encounter into a lecture.
But she also does not allow the action to cross the other without containment.
If the gesture begins to hurt, the entry is clear. To protect — not to punish.
The adult holds the arm. Separates the bodies. Reduces the force. Gives contour to the movement. The limit appears as care.
The child feels this as a change in the environment.

The gesture that was coming whole encounters resistance. The action needs to reorganize itself in order to continue. A step back. A moment of waiting. A minimal displacement that avoids the direct collision.

That adjustment is born from lived experience. The child discovers, by doing, that there is a possible intensity and another that stops everything. That continuing demands modulation. That the other feels the effect of the gesture.

None of this is named as a moral lesson. It is lived as experience. Something begins to transform. The other’s presence stops being only a barrier. It begins to be part of the terrain. The child perceives that she does not cross the space the same way when someone is there. That running demands detours. That taking demands waiting. That continuing demands adjusting the force.

That process does not happen all at once. Nor in a linear way. On some days, the adjustment comes quickly. On others, the impulse returns whole. The adult remains. Sustains. Contains when necessary. Releases when possible. Does not give up on the experience.
Because learning only builds itself when there is enough repetition for the gesture to recognize the limit without feeling erased.
When the adult resolves everything too early, the child does not live the adjustment. When she withdraws too far, the encounter becomes a threat. The point is in the middle.
With repetition, signals appear. The child brakes before colliding. Pulls back her hand at the last second. Reduces force. Looks to see if someone is there. The gesture changes before the impact.
That is a silent milestone. Autonomy begins to take another form — it is no longer only doing alone, but continuing to be who one is with the other present.

The action stops being solitary. The doing becomes coordinated. The adult notices when the child no longer collapses before the limit. When she manages to wait. When she adjusts the gesture without losing interest. When the encounter transforms instead of interrupting.
That learning does not call attention. But it is what makes coexistence possible.
Because the world does not step aside for the child to pass. It asks for curves.
And learning to make curves without disappearing is one of the deepest gestures of living autonomy — an autonomy that coexists.

Acting together asks more than acting alone. It asks for perceiving the limit, sustaining the pause, and finding a force that allows continuing without hurting. It is in that adjustment that action becomes truly shared.

items.title: When another child enters the situation, observe the exact instant of impact: the gaze that changes, the gesture that stiffens, the acceleration or the freezing.
When faced with the freezing, try sustaining presence for a few moments before speaking or acting. Not every discomfort asks for immediate correction.
items.text: Entering only when the limit becomes risk

items.title: If the gesture begins to cross the other with force, the entry is clear. To protect.

cap-14.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-14.subtitle: Feeling the time of adjustment
body: Remember a recent situation in which someone changed your rhythm: interrupted your speech, crossed your path, grabbed something before you.
Notice: where did the reaction arise first? What happened right after? How much time was needed for adjustment?
Now imagine someone had resolved the situation for you before that adjustment could happen. Notice the difference.
Many times, that is exactly the interval — brief, uncomfortable, and precious — that the child is learning to cross.

cap-14.text: The other does not interrupt the action. He invites a different way of continuing.
When the child begins to adjust the gesture without disappearing, something new is announced. Identity begins to exist in relation to the other. That is where we follow.

cap-15.text: In the previous chapter, the challenge was to adjust the force when bodies met physically — to modulate movement, contain impulse, protect the other without disappearing. Here, the challenge is of another nature: sustaining one’s own axis when the other enters the doing that organizes the child. It is about continuing to exist when the play that holds her is touched by another will.
The child plays. The activity is known. The gesture repeats. She finds pleasure and organization in what she already knows how to do.
There is another child nearby. She participates. She follows the rhythm. She uses the same objects. The play happens without tension because the path remains stable.
While the doing follows that known axis, being together is possible.
What sustains that proximity is the continuity of the action. The play works. Pleasure organizes.
At a certain moment, that changes.
The other alters the path. She introduces a variation. She changes the rule. She runs in another direction. The play stops responding to what the child knows.

What is lost is the stability of the doing. The gesture that held the shared presence stops working. The child tries to insist. She repeats the known sequence. She tries to bring the game back to the axis that organizes her.
When that does not happen, she retreats. Not always does that retreat lead to another structured activity. Many times, it leads to a withdrawal.
The child steps back, finds a corner, begins a repetitive movement, or simply stops playing.
It is an attempt at reorganization when faced with an experience that lost coherence.
It is at that point that the adult’s presence becomes decisive. Not to push the child back toward the play that came apart. Nor to leave her isolated in the void.
The adult offers an activity the child knows and that tends to organize her. A familiar game. An object that sustains the gesture. A doing that restores direction.
The invitation happens first for the child. When she returns to movement and pleasure begins to reorganize itself, the adult widens the field.
The adult announces the activity to the others. Invites participation. Introduces the other in a mediated way — protecting the axis of the play.

That entry is not spontaneous. It is sustained. The child may reject. May feel disturbed. May try to push the other away. The adult remains. Regulates the approach. Limits excesses. Prevents abrupt invasions.

The other does not enter freely. The other enters with contour. With the repetition of those experiences, something consolidates. The child begins to tolerate the other’s presence within an activity that organizes her — as long as that activity is preserved.
That is remaining. Identity begins to firm itself exactly there: in the possibility of continuing to do what holds even when someone is nearby.
The other stops being only an obstacle. The other becomes a possible presence within a protected doing.
This chapter speaks of holding one’s own axis so that being together is not lived as a threat.

That process does not transform solitary play into shared play immediately. What is built is the possibility of remaining — remaining in the activity that holds even when another body approaches, without needing to interrupt, flee, or defend oneself. The other’s presence becomes tolerable because it does not threaten the axis that organizes the doing. It is at that level — concrete, bodily, repeated — that identity begins to gain consistency.

When that base firms itself, something essential becomes available for the next movements of development. The child begins to recognize that she can exist in the world without needing to disappear for the other to exist.
The encounter stops being lived only as a risk of loss and begins to be sustained as a possible experience — by enough internal stability.
It is from that ground that other forms of being together will be able, further ahead, to take shape.
Being someone, here, is continuing to exist without getting lost when the world stops being only one’s own.

items.title: When the child withdraws because the game changed, sustain the interval. Not every retreat asks for immediate correction.
When disorganization is perceived, approach with something the child recognizes and that tends to reorganize the gesture.
When play reestablishes itself, use your own presence to invite others to approach that territory.

cap-15.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-15.subtitle: The value of the invitation
body: Remember a situation in which you felt displaced in a group. Now imagine someone approaching — not to correct or redirect, but to propose exactly what you know how to do — and inviting others to participate.
Observe the effect. Many times, that is the safety the adult offers when she transforms the child’s retreat into the possibility of encounter.

cap-15.text: The interest that organizes the gesture can become a bridge. The adult only keeps that bridge visible for long enough.

When the child perceives that she can sustain who she is and still be accompanied, something new begins to take shape. The other begins to appear as someone distinct — with desires, initiatives, and rhythms of their own. That is where we follow.

cap-16.text: The object is there. It is not just any one.
It is that specific element that calls the child before becoming thought. She looks, orients herself, approaches. The gesture is direct, safe — it has traveled that path many times.
Until there, the world responded. Now, something changes. The object is not free. There is a presence in the middle. A body that arrived first. A hand that holds. A movement that occupies the space.

The child extends her arm. The gesture encounters resistance. There is still no social reading. No calculation of intention. There is only a new piece of information: the path does not work as before.
She tries again. Adjusts the angle. Approaches further. The arm insists — not to impose, but to restore the known logic: if I arrive, I take.
The other reacts. Perhaps holds with more force. Perhaps pulls back. Perhaps stiffens or raises their voice.
That reaction is felt as interruption. The impact appears first in the child. The rhythm breaks. The gesture loses continuity. Something that was predictable stops sustaining the action.

This is a world that does not respond. At that point, the child is not yet trying to share. She is trying to make things work. The desire is instrumental. The object remains the focus. The other occupies the place of obstacle.
When the reaction intensifies — a push, a cry, a sob — a new element enters the experience as a strong signal: the action cannot continue in the same way.
Here, the adult’s intervention is decisive. Not to convince. Not to moralize. Not to resolve quickly.
The adult enters to translate the limit into gesture. She approaches. The hand contains. The force is reduced. The space reorganizes. Little is said. Sometimes, nothing.
The object can be removed for a moment. Can be placed out of reach. Can be held between the bodies as a visible reference.
The focus is not the toy. It is the experience. The child begins to live something new: acting does not guarantee result.
That builds itself through repetition. At one moment, she erupts. At another, she stiffens and stops — or simply withdraws in search of something predictable.
All of that is part of the process.
The adult does not transform that interruption into personal rejection. Nor into guilt. Nor into a lesson.
She sustains the direct experience: the gesture does not always find its return.
With time — and only with time — something begins to shift. The child pauses before insisting. Observes the object in the other’s hand. Tolerates, for a few seconds, the waiting.
There is no understanding of the reason. There is sustaining of the effect.
That is the central gain of that moment of development — the initial capacity to remain when action does not produce the expected result.

That learning happens through the repeated experience of encountering the limit. She learns, little by little, that insisting does not always reorganize the world. Pausing, withdrawing, or waiting can become a way of continuing to exist when action does not find an immediate response.
It is on that ground that something fundamental establishes itself: the possibility of remaining even when the previous logic no longer sustains the doing — as inner reorganization, not as giving up.
That is the point from which the other will be able, further ahead, to begin to be perceived as someone with their own intention.
The child needs to cross the experience that not everything responds to her own gesture before being able to understand the other.

items.title: When the gesture begins to escalate, the adult’s entry aims to contain.
The object can be removed — but the adult’s presence remains as a stable reference.
The other’s state is not named. Experience comes before understanding.

cap-16.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-16.subtitle: When something does not respond
body: Remember a situation in which something simple stopped working. A button that does not turn on. A door that does not open.
Observe the reaction before the thought. That is where the child is.

cap-16.text: The challenge is not the other. It is when the logic that held the world stops working.
When the child begins to sustain that the world does not respond as before, a new movement is announced. The other begins to gain intention. That is where we follow.

cap-17.text: When the child begins to tolerate that action does not always produce the same result, something new begins to happen. Not suddenly. Not in an organized way. But repeated enough to leave marks.
In activities she already masters, the other’s presence begins to interfere with how the doing functions. The response does not come. The rule changes. The sequence breaks.

Those interruptions stop being isolated episodes. They become recurrent. The child begins to notice that it is not the object that stops working, nor only the gesture — it is the other’s presence that introduces variation.
Something new emerges: the need to follow what the other does so that the action can work again.
It is at that point that the other stops being only an obstacle and begins, slowly, to become a reference. As something that needs to be observed.
The child looks. To predict — not to connect. The gaze arises as strategy.
The gesture pauses for a slightly longer moment. It waits before happening. There is following.
The other enters the field as an active variable. Someone whose doing alters the course of what is happening.

This can occur in movement games, when the other’s rhythm changes. It can occur in table games, when a piece is not placed where expected. It can occur in simple activities, when the other does it differently without warning.
The common point is not the type of activity. It is the repetition of interference.

The child begins to perceive that, for something to work, it is not enough to repeat the gesture. It is necessary to take the other into account — so that the action continues, not to please or to adapt.

That displacement is deep — and still fragile. At some moments, the gaze appears. At others, it disappears. The child may observe attentively on certain days and, on others, return to the automatic gesture.
All of that is part of the process. What matters is that the other is no longer invisible. Not yet understood. Accompanied.

Accompanying is already an immense step. Here, the adult’s role continues to be sustaining the field. Without explaining what the other thinks. Without translating intentions. Without anticipating conclusions.
The adult allows observation to happen. Allows time to extend itself. Allows action to reorganize around that new variable.
Empathy is not requested. Understanding is not required. The space is protected where looking is still enough.
Because it is from that place — still bodily, still pre-conceptual — that something larger can be born.

That movement does not transform observation into immediate interaction. What is built, first, is the capacity to adjust one’s own gesture from what the other does — without needing to interrupt the action completely.

The reference is still not affective or symbolic. It is functional. The other begins to exist because he alters the path of the doing — and that is already enough for the gaze to find its place in the process.
It is at that level, repeated and sustained, that the other’s presence begins to inscribe itself as a real element of the world that needs to be considered for action to continue being possible.
The child needs to notice that he interferes before being able to understand the other. As something that changes the course of action — not yet as someone to be understood.
When the other’s behavior begins to be taken into account — still without meaning, still without a name — the world stops being only things. It begins, slowly, to become relationship.

items.title: When the child observes the other before acting, avoid ending the activity quickly. The time of observation is part of the process.
If the child follows the other’s gesture, do not attribute meanings. Meaning comes later; now it is experience.
Allow small changes when the other enters. Variation is what invites the gaze to exist.

cap-17.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-17.subtitle: When observing becomes a necessity
body: Remember a situation in which something that worked well stopped working because of another person — not by intention, but by difference of action.
Notice when the need to observe arose. Not out of interest — but to predict the next step.
It is from that place that the gaze begins to organize itself.

cap-17.text: The other does not begin to exist when he is understood. He begins to exist when he interferes.

Observing is not yet interacting. Before direct relationship, many children seek an intermediate territory where intentions can be tested without risk. It is at that point that the toy begins to become a rehearsal. That is where we follow.

cap-18.text: Throughout the last few chapters, something was building itself. The child encountered the other — not as an idea, but as concrete presence. Another hand wanting the same object. Another rhythm crossing the play. Another will altering the path.
That encounter demanded real coordination. Adjusting force. Observing the other’s movement. Tolerating the occupied object. That learning happened. But not without cost.

Coordinating with someone alive — full of their own initiatives and unforeseen changes — demands more than many children can sustain continuously. At some moments, they accompany. At others, they retreat. Not from rejection — from exhaustion. Maintaining constant coordination is intense work.
It is at that point that an intermediate territory appears.
A space where the other can begin to exist without being physically present. Where another’s agency can be rehearsed without the risk of real unpredictability.

That place is the toy. For a long time, the toy was only an object. It turned, fit together, opened, closed. The gesture always produced the same effect. The world obeyed form. That functional play continues as ground — it does not disappear. It is the ground where movement finds rhythm and predictability.
But at some moment, the object begins to carry something beyond itself.

A block slides across the floor. It can be a car. A box becomes a house. A cloth becomes a blanket. The gesture remains, but meaning folds itself. The object stops responding only to its physical form and begins to sustain another layer of meaning.
The adult accompanies with silent attention. Does not explain too much. Does not transform the gesture into a long narrative. Only validates that something can exist in two layers at the same time.

That is the beginning. With time, the object begins to do things. The doll rises, falls, gets up. The toy car hits, retreats, tries again. The action gains sequence. There is beginning, middle, and end. Repetition organizes time and creates predictability within variation.

And then something essential begins to prepare itself. The doll wants to climb. The toy car tries to pass. The animal waits. The adult can lend a simple voice to what is happening. Only intention joined to gesture:
“He is looking. He does not know where it is.” “He looks inside the box. He thinks it is there.” “He waits. He thinks someone will open.”

Those are simple sentences, still joined to action. But now they carry another layer: the gesture begins to have its origin in a thought. The doll acts because it thinks, because it knows, because it believes.
The child can accept that. Can ignore it. Can continue playing as before. The adult does not force. She only deposits the hypothesis — always joined to what is happening.
With repetition, something begins to inscribe itself. The doll has interiority.
A simple interiority, that can be tested and modulated still in the protected territory of play.
Here, the child does not need to deal with the unpredictable thoughts of another real person. She can rehearse that idea in the doll, where the rhythm continues under control.
And when the doll can think, another tool can help to sustain that movement.
Social stories. They are short narratives that describe concrete situations and connect behavior to inner states. Not as lists of rules — but as maps of functioning.
A social story does not only say what happened. It links the gesture to what precedes it from within.
“The teacher raises her hand. She wants attention. When the class notices, they stop talking. She feels satisfied because she got what she needed.”
The gesture is visible. What holds it is not. The narrative builds that bridge.
Another example: “João smiles when he sees me at the park. He likes playing with me. When I smile back, he feels happy. He notices that I also want to play.”
Here, what organizes itself is not only behavior. It is the idea that people act from what they feel or imagine.
Stories help to become familiar with that idea — that there is something internal orienting behavior, including one’s own.

With time and repetition, the child may begin to notice that people do things for reasons that are not on show. That they may search for something because they believe it is in a place — even when it is not. That they may act from what they think, and not only from what is visible.
This does not arise all at once. Nor in the same way for all children.

Some develop that understanding in an intuitive way, even if delayed. Others construct inferences in a more rational way. Others remain with partial understanding — they sustain one layer, but not all. All of that is possible development.
What matters is not to force — but to offer conditions so that, if it can emerge, it finds sustaining.
Make-believe offers that space when it allows the doll to have interiority. Stories offer that space when they translate what does not appear in the gesture.
It is preparation. Ground where something can, further ahead, form itself.
The child needs to be able to sustain the idea that the other’s thought exists — before having to read it in the unpredictable rhythm of coexistence.
She needs to imagine that someone can think differently. Act from something that does not correspond to reality. Believe in something she does not believe.
When that becomes possible, even in protected form, something fundamental is built.
The other stops being only a body that acts and becomes someone who acts because they think, because they feel, because they suppose something about the world.
That is one of the most sophisticated movements of human development. That is why it is not rushed. Not transformed into a rigid goal. Not measured as an obligatory achievement.

Time is respected. Support is offered. Space is created. And when that understanding begins to arise — even if partially, even if with effort — the relationship with the real other gains new resources.
The child can begin to consider what moves the other. What he thinks. What he supposes. Why he acts.
That does not eliminate the cost of interaction. It does not make the encounter simple.
But it makes it possible to take into account that something is happening inside the other.
The other begins to gain depth. And when that happens, the path opens.

items.title: The repeated gesture is ground. Do not rush the transformation. The symbolic needs predictable ground to arise.
If the block becomes a car, accompany with presence. Do not explain too much. Do not transform the moment into a lesson.
Name only the intention linked to the gesture: “He wants to climb.” “He tries to pass.” “He waits.” Avoid complex emotions.
Beginning. Middle. End. Three chained movements already organize time.

cap-18.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-18.subtitle: Where the other can exist without threatening
body: Think of a social situation that usually tires you.
Now imagine that same situation with characters that you control. They have wills — but you can modulate them.
Notice the difference. Make-believe offers the child exactly that: a space where the other can begin to exist without costing more than she can sustain.

cap-18.text: The child needs to be able to imagine the other without losing her own axis before understanding him in real relationship.
When the other can exist in the toy, something prepares itself silently. The other’s mind begins to gain contour — first in safety, then in real presence. That is where we follow.

cap-19.text: When the doll can want, something prepares itself.
In the previous chapter, the toy gained agency. The doll wants to climb. The toy car tries to pass. The animal waits. Those are simple intentions, visible, linked to gesture.
But wanting is not yet thinking. Trying is not yet believing. Waiting is not yet knowing.

There is a difference between perceiving that someone wants something and perceiving that someone thinks something. The first can be seen in the body. The second happens from within — it does not appear directly, it needs to be imagined.

It is in that delicate terrain that this chapter moves. Understanding the other is not only recognizing what he does. It is sustaining that something is happening inside him — something that orients what he does, even when that is not explicit.
For many children, that step is one of the most complex in development. The other’s inner world can remain too abstract for a long time.

So, how to make it more accessible? Make-believe can take a new step. When the doll can already want, the adult can introduce something more. The doll does not only want. He can also know — or not know.
“He is looking. He does not know where it is.” “He looks inside the box. He thinks it is there.” “He waits. He thinks someone will open.”
Those are simple sentences, still linked to action. But now they carry another layer: the gesture has its origin in a thought. The doll acts because it thinks, because it knows, because it believes.
The child can accept that. Can ignore it. Can continue playing as before. The adult does not force. She only deposits the hypothesis — always joined to what is happening.
With repetition, something begins to inscribe itself. The doll has interiority.

In the previous chapter, social stories were introduced as a first bridge — linking gesture to intention. Here, they go one step further: from intention to thought. The doll no longer only wants — it also believes, supposes, and knows. And the story makes that invisible layer visible.
A social story does not only say what happened. It links the gesture to what precedes it from within — to a thought, a belief, a state that oriented the action before it was visible.
“The teacher raises her hand. She wants attention. When the class notices, they stop talking. She feels satisfied because she got what she needed.”
The gesture is visible. The thought that produced it is not. The narrative builds that bridge — between what can be seen and what can only be imagined.
Another example: “João smiles when he sees me at the park. He likes playing with me. When I smile back, he feels happy. He notices that I also want to play.”
Here, what organizes itself is not only behavior. It is the idea that people act from what they feel or imagine — from something happening inside them that cannot be seen directly, only inferred.
Stories help to become familiar with that idea — that there is something internal orienting behavior, including one’s own.

With time and repetition, the child may begin to notice that people do things for reasons that are not on show. That they may search for something because they believe it is in a place — even when it is not. That they may act from what they think, and not only from what is visible.
This does not arise all at once. Nor in the same way for all children.

Some develop that understanding in an intuitive way, even if delayed. Others construct inferences in a more rational way. Others remain with partial understanding — they sustain one layer, but not all.
All of that is possible development. What matters is not to force — but to offer conditions so that, if it can emerge, it finds sustaining.
Make-believe offers that space when it allows the doll to have interiority. Stories offer that space when they translate what does not appear in the gesture.
It is preparation. Ground where something can, further ahead, form itself.
The child needs to be able to sustain the idea that the other’s thought exists — before having to read it in the unpredictable rhythm of coexistence.
She needs to imagine that someone can think differently. Act from something that does not correspond to reality. Believe in something she does not believe.
When that becomes possible, even in protected form, something fundamental is built.
The other stops being only a body that acts and becomes someone who acts because they think, because they feel, because they suppose something about the world.
That is one of the most sophisticated movements of human development. That is why it is not rushed. Not transformed into a rigid goal. Not measured as an obligatory achievement.

Time is respected. Support is offered. Space is created. And when that understanding begins to arise — even if partially, even if with effort — the relationship with the real other gains new resources.
The child can begin to consider what moves the other. What he thinks. What he supposes. Why he acts.
That does not eliminate the cost of interaction. It does not make the encounter simple.
But it makes it possible to take into account that something is happening inside the other.
The other begins to gain depth. And when that happens, the path opens.

items.title: When the doll acts, name what it thinks: “He is looking. He does not know where it is.” “He looks there. He thinks he found it.” Always connecting thought and action.
items.text: Using stories to map what happens inside

items.title: Short narratives that link gesture → thought → consequence. Not as a rule. As translation.
Familiarization comes through repetition. The pattern inscribes itself gradually.
Avoid asking “did you understand?” The stories enter as experience, not as a lesson.

cap-19.title: VIVENTIAL EXERCISE
cap-19.subtitle: When something needs to be explained from inside
body: Think of a situation in which you did not understand why someone acted in a certain way. The gesture was clear. The reason was not.
Now imagine someone explaining: “She did that because she thought you already knew. When she realized you did not know, she felt embarrassed.”
Notice how the explanation reorganizes the experience. For many children, the whole social world can seem like that: visible actions, non-apparent reasons. Stories help to build that bridge.

cap-19.text: The other gains depth when he can think, want, and know — not only act. That is a delicate step. When it happens, it happens slowly. Always in relationship.

When the other’s interiority begins to be considered, the adult occupies a new place. Not as the one who conducts each step — but as the one who holds the field where that understanding continues to organize itself. That is where we follow, in Chapter 20.

cap-20.text: Throughout this book, the focus has been on the child — on what she lives, on what she needs, on what she builds.

Now, at the end of this path, the gaze turns to whoever accompanies. Because something has also changed on the side of those who care. It was not a new technique. Not a set of strategies. Nor a method to be applied mechanically.

It was the form of seeing. At the beginning, perhaps everything seemed confusing. The child did things that did not fit into ready explanations. She repeated, insisted, withdrew, returned, collapsed, reorganized. The other — whether a peer, an adult, or the environment itself — appeared, many times, more as noise than as support.

Chapter by chapter, the scene gained contour. It became clear that nothing there was random. Every gesture had function. Every withdrawal was an attempt at preservation. Every insistence, a way of keeping the logic alive.
Development stopped appearing as a linear staircase. It began to reveal itself as a process in movement.
The child does not simply “advance.” She negotiates. She negotiates with the body. With objects. With the other’s presence. With limits she does not yet understand — but already feels.
In accompanying that path, the adult stopped searching for immediate answers and began to read processes.
This is the true legacy of the book. It is not knowing what to do in each situation. It is knowing what is at stake.

It became possible to distinguish when the child is regulating the body and when she is only trying to make the action work. It became possible to recognize the moment when she preserves a silent axis — and the moment when she begins, still unstably, to rehearse the other in the safety of play.
This reading changes the adult’s place. The reaction stops being to visible behavior and begins to respond to the level of development active in that instant.
It is here that something shifts. The adult stops occupying only the place of the one who cares, protects, or carries out external guidance. They begin to coordinate.
They coordinate the environment. Time. The entry and exit of stimuli. The presence of other adults. And, when necessary, the articulation with professionals.
Not as someone who knows everything. But as someone who accompanies the process from within.

It becomes possible to perceive when an intervention helps — and when it only anticipates something that still needs to be lived. When an explanation is premature. When a limit is necessary. When silence holds more than any word.
This knowledge does not come from outside. It builds itself in the relationship.

In accompanying development without skipping stages, without romanticizing, and without transforming every difficulty into absence, something concrete happens: the adult no longer listens to professionals as someone receiving absolute truths — but neither do they dismiss them.

They dialogue. They formulate more precise questions. They name what they observe in daily life. They notice when approaches do not speak to each other. They recognize when a proposal respects — or overrides — the child’s real moment.
The adult does not become a specialist.
They become an axis.

They are the one who sees the child wake up, play, collapse, reorganize, try again. They are the one who notices micro-changes that do not appear in reports. They are the one who feels when something begins to make sense — or when something begins to break internally.
This place is not comfortable. But it is alive. Development does not happen in isolated sessions. It happens in the between.
Between home and school. Between therapy and daily life. Between intention and result. Between what already works and what still needs to organize itself.
This final chapter does not propose replacing professionals. It proposes something more demanding: to articulate.
To articulate needs, times, languages, and expectations. Without hurry. Without recipes. Without illusions of control.
The book ends here.
The path does not.
There is now a lens. Not to label — but to accompany.
And that changes, in a silent and profound way, the manner of walking alongside the child.

autor.text: Ihave been working for nearly three decades in special and inclusive education, as a teacher and educational therapist, accompanying autistic children, families, and educators. Over that time, I have worked in very different contexts — Brazil, the United Kingdom, and Portugal — changing language, educational system, and public policy. But something never changed: the silence that tends to form around adults when they receive a diagnosis and do not know, in practice, what to do with it.

I have seen confused parents facing reports that do not speak to each other. I have seen overburdened teachers trying to apply strategies disconnected from the reality of the classroom. I have seen competent but fragmented professionals, each looking at one part of the child — rarely at the whole.

And I have seen, above all, children trying to exist in that middle. Over the years, it became clear to me that the greatest gap was not between the child and the world — but between the lived experience and the language used to explain it.
What was missing was someone who could help adults see development not as a list of skills to be trained — but as a living, bodily, relational process.
This book is born from that place.

It was not written to teach techniques, nor to replace professionals. It was written to return to the adult a role that is often taken from them: that of the attentive observer, the articulator, the axis of the process.
Someone capable of dialoguing with therapists, understanding reports, questioning approaches — and, at the same time, trusting what they see and feel in daily life with the child.

My training is interdisciplinary, with a strong base in body-based work, child development, and special education. But more than titles, what holds this book is years of listening: to the bodies of children, to the families that walk alongside, and to the educators who remain when the initial enthusiasm has passed.
The idea that runs through the entire work — and that also orients the GrowKind World project — is simple and demanding:
Development does not happen in isolation, nor does it resolve in sessions. It happens in the between.
Between people. Between times. Between attempts that fail and reorganize themselves.
I write for parents who want to understand, not only to apply. For teachers who feel something is missing beyond technique. For professionals who wish to work in partnership, not in hierarchy.
And I write because I believe that when the adult begins to see, the child no longer has to carry alone the weight of adapting to the world.
